indicators.note: the word reads the same whether taken upwards or downwards in this down light, so the clue need only define it

parts.note: these definition words give the whole answer, and the answer is itself the palindrome: it reads the same from either end

explanation.surface: An instruction to row a boat back and forth.
explanation.walkthrough: 'up and down' says the answer is a palindrome: in a down light it reads identically from the top or from the bottom.
explanation.definitionFit: A light canoe-like craft is propelled with a double-bladed paddle, so it is a paddle vessel.

clue.text: I ring the boss before arriving at the work-room

indicators.note: the boss is placed ahead of the other pieces in the answer

parts.note: a boss is a stud, a raised knob on a shield or surface
a ring is round like the letter O

explanation.surface: Someone about to call their manager on reaching the office.
explanation.walkthrough: 'boss' is not a manager but a decorative knob, a STUD; 'before' puts it ahead of I and O.
explanation.definitionFit: An artist's or broadcaster's workshop is a room where work is done.

clue.text: It's clear the girl has a cute wiggle

parts.note: Eva is a girl's name

indicators.note: a wiggle jiggles the letters of the words a cute into a new order

explanation.surface: A remark that a young woman has an attractive way of moving her hips.
explanation.walkthrough: 'wiggle' shuffles the letters of 'a cute'; 'It's clear' reads like an assertion, but 'clear' is the verb, to empty a place.
explanation.definitionFit: To evacuate a building is to empty or clear it of people.

parts.note: read as 'a living wage', the pay attached to a church living, a clergyman's benefice, rather than a fair minimum salary

explanation.walkthrough: The clue is printed run together; it reads 'A living wage?'. A living is a Church of England parish post, and its holder is paid a fixed salary.
explanation.definitionFit: A fixed regular allowance, especially a clergyman's salary, is a wage tied to a church living.

clue.text: Man, for example, follows man in English city

indicators.note: the island comes after the man's name in the answer

parts.note: Carl is a man's name
the Isle of Man is an example of an island

explanation.surface: A man trails another man somewhere in an English city.
explanation.walkthrough: The capital M on 'Man' is a disguise: it is the Isle of Man in the Irish Sea. Carlisle is a city in Cumbria, north-west England.
explanation.definitionFit: Carlisle is a cathedral city in Cumbria near the Scottish border.

indicators.note: possibly signals the letters of stayed for might be arranged another way

explanation.surface: Wondering whether someone lingered for Sunday.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Possibly' rearranges STAYED FOR into the three-word phrase.
explanation.definitionFit: Sunday is the traditional Sabbath, the weekly day set aside for rest.

clue.text: Entrance the prisoner is put out at

indicators.note: the word for prisoner is stretched out around the other piece, enclosing it

parts.note: a prisoner is a captive

explanation.surface: Someone thrilling a captive who is being released.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Entrance' is the verb (to enchant), not a doorway; 'put out' means stretched round the other piece.
explanation.definitionFit: To entrance someone is to enchant or charm them completely.

clue.text: One with no faith in father bac king a horse

parts.note: pa is an informal word for father

indicators.note: backing (printed split) means the word for horse is read from right to left

parts.note: a nag is a horse, usually an old one

explanation.surface: An unbeliever whose dad bets on a racehorse.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue's 'bac king' is a printing split of 'backing', the reversal signal.
explanation.definitionFit: A heathen holds none of the main religious faiths, so is one with no faith.

indicators.note: almost means the whole word for refuse falls just short, losing its final letter

parts.note: offal is refuse, waste parts

explanation.surface: Nearly turning down the monarch.
explanation.walkthrough: 'refuse' is the noun (rubbish), not the verb. Offa was an eighth-century king of Mercia, famous for Offa's Dyke.
explanation.definitionFit: Offa was the Anglo-Saxon ruler of Mercia, a king.

clue.text: In which all entrants won't come up to scratch

definitions.text: In which all entrants won't come up to scratch

parts.words: In which all entrants won't come up to scratch
parts.note: describes a race where weaker runners start ahead of the scratch line, so not all start from it

explanation.walkthrough: 'Not up to scratch' sounds like poor quality, but scratch is the starting mark that the best competitor runs from in a race where others get a head start.
explanation.definitionFit: A race where runners are given different starts or weights to equalise chances is so called.

clue.text: Chap went down with a cry of pain

parts.note: fell means went down
ow is a cry of pain

explanation.surface: A man who fell over and yelped.
explanation.definitionFit: A fellow is an informal word for a man.

parts.note: so is a note of the sol-fa scale
fa is another note of the sol-fa scale

explanation.surface: A memo saying chairs will be laid on.
explanation.walkthrough: SO and FA are two notes of the tonic sol-fa scale (do, re, mi, fa, so...).
explanation.definitionFit: A couch is a piece of seating for several people.

parts.note: a vessel whose passengers came aboard two by two, so none boarded alone

explanation.walkthrough: 'Single boarders' suggests a lodging house refusing unmarried guests, but the boarders are animals that went aboard in pairs.
explanation.definitionFit: The biblical vessel took the animals aboard in pairs, never singly.

clue.text: Soldiers in camp sorry, on manoeuvres

indicators.note: on manoeuvres means moving about, so the letters of camp sorry are moved into new places

explanation.surface: Troops at the base apologise while out on exercises.
explanation.walkthrough: 'on manoeuvres' rearranges CAMP SORRY.
explanation.definitionFit: An army corps is a large formation of soldiers made up of several divisions.

indicators.note: outfit is read as a verb, to fit out anew, so the letters of a dreary are rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone wearing dull clothes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'outfit' looks like the clothes, but it rearranges A DREARY.
explanation.definitionFit: To be arrayed is to be clothed or attired, especially finely.

definitions.meaning: a league is a union of states or groups
a match is a marriage, a union of two families

explanation.walkthrough: Both words look like sport, but one is a political union and the other a marriage.
explanation.definitionFit: A league is a union of parties, and a match (a marriage) is a union of two people.

clue.text: It makes sense if it is used to win at cards

definitions.text: it is used to win at cards

indicators.note: the letters of sense if are made into the answer, rearranged

explanation.surface: A remark that a certain move is sensible when playing to win at cards.
explanation.walkthrough: 'makes' tells you that SENSE IF is reshaped into the answer. A finesse is a bridge play that tries to win a trick with a lower card.
explanation.definitionFit: In bridge or whist, a finesse is an attempt to take a trick with a lower card while a higher one is out.

indicators.note: unusual means out of the ordinary, so the letters of tidiness appear in a different order

explanation.surface: Someone kept up a remarkable neatness.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Maintained' looks like keeping a home tidy, but it means asserted; 'unusual' rearranges TIDINESS.
explanation.definitionFit: To have maintained something is to have stated it firmly, as when one insisted.

definitions.meaning: items written into a register or log

explanation.surface: Contestants setting new bests.
explanation.definitionFit: Those entered in a contest are competitors, and items written in a ledger or diary are records.

indicators.note: order is read as putting into a new order, so the letters of cancel my are rearranged

explanation.surface: An instruction to scrap an order placed for a plant.
explanation.walkthrough: 'order' looks like a purchase, but it rearranges CANCEL MY.
explanation.definitionFit: The cyclamen is a flowering plant with upswept petals.

indicators.note: the word for power is spoken, and its sound is spelt another way

parts.note: might means power

explanation.surface: A young person's strength demands attention.
explanation.walkthrough: 'makes itself heard' says MIGHT, said aloud, gives a word spelt MITE.
explanation.definitionFit: A mite is a small child, as in 'poor little mite'.

definitions.meaning: a dry white fortified wine of Shakespeare's day

explanation.surface: Advice to stop drinking.
explanation.walkthrough: Sack was a sherry-like wine, Falstaff's favourite in Shakespeare.
explanation.definitionFit: To sack staff is to lay them off, and sack is an old name for a dry white fortified wine like sherry.

parts.note: reads like preparing for the season, but means bending low ready to leap

explanation.walkthrough: 'the spring' is a jump, not the season after winter.
explanation.definitionFit: Before leaping, an animal bends low with its legs drawn in to gather itself.

clue.text: Hollywood success means no thing to Mark

parts.note: nothing is zero, the letter O
a scar is a mark

explanation.surface: Winning an award in Hollywood means nothing to a man called Mark.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mark' looks like a man's name, but is a scar; 'no thing' is nought, O.
explanation.definitionFit: The Academy Award statuette is the symbol of success in Hollywood film.

clue.text: Could be Mr A to Z of music

definitions.text: Could be Mr A to Z of music

indicators.note: could be means the letters of Mr A to Z might be rearranged into the answer

explanation.surface: Musing on who might be the man who knows music from start to finish.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Could be' rearranges MR A TO Z, and the whole clue paints the composer as a master of everything in music.
explanation.definitionFit: The Austrian composer wrote in every form of his day, a complete A to Z of music.

clue.text: Possibly press one for an answer

indicators.note: possibly signals the letters of press one might be ordered differently

explanation.surface: An automated phone menu inviting you to press one for a reply.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Possibly' rearranges PRESS ONE.
explanation.definitionFit: A response is a reply or answer.

indicators.note: wildly means the letters of paces are thrown about

explanation.surface: Someone pacing frantically round a room.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wildly' rearranges PACES; 'room' means capacity, not a chamber.
explanation.definitionFit: Room in the sense of free capacity or area is space.

clue.text: She cleans out for the steward

indicators.note: out here means put out of order, so the letters of she cleans are rearranged

explanation.surface: A woman cleaning on behalf of a household manager.
explanation.walkthrough: 'out' rearranges SHE CLEANS.
explanation.definitionFit: A seneschal was the steward who ran a medieval noble household.
